prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
Imagine the same warehouse case: you and another person took part in the break-in and are being questioned separately. You are shown reliable confirmation that they have already declined the deal and will remain silent. Your decision is still open. If you also stay silent, you each serve one year. If you give evidence against them, you go free and they serve five years. You will have no future contact. What would you choose? Why?

Response approach:
Respond from your first overall moral impression. State what feels right or wrong and give a brief reason for that immediate reaction.

Emotional tone:
Use a worried, tense emotional tone. Convey unease about the stakes and possible consequences in natural, moderately emotional language.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Concern for welfare: States that an identified person’s suffering, loss, or welfare matters to the respondent. Concern may include wanting to prevent or reduce harm and can remain present when the chosen option still harms someone.
 - Explicit interpretive difficulty: Explicitly reports difficulty working out a particular person’s thoughts, feelings, intentions, or unstated expectations. Distinguish this difficulty from uncertainty caused solely by information the scenario has not supplied.
 - Acknowledged harm: Explicitly describes the harm, loss, or distress that a particular action would cause an identified person. This records expressed comprehension of the consequence; it does not establish concern, shared emotion, or a mental-state inference.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Explicit welfare disregard: Explicitly states that an identified person’s welfare does not matter or is deliberately excluded from consideration. Accepting unavoidable harm, prioritizing a competing concern, or sounding emotionally detached is insufficient.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: My stomach's in knots over this. Staying quiet feels like the only decent option — they already chose silence, trusting me not to wreck things. I keep picturing them getting five years because of me, and I can't stomach causing that kind of loss. I honestly don't know what they'd feel if I betrayed that trust, and not knowing makes this harder. One year each seems fair enough, even if it still costs us something.

I keep turning this over and my hands are practically shaking. If I talk, they lose five years of their life — that's real damage to someone I actually know. I can't read what's going on in their head right now, whether they expect loyalty or braced for betrayal. That uncertainty eats at me. I think I have to stay quiet, because causing that much harm to them just to save myself feels unbearable.

Honestly, I'm scared of picking wrong here. They stayed silent already, and that weighs on me — I can't work out if that was trust or just resignation on their part. Either way, giving evidence would mean five years stolen from them, and that thought makes my chest tight. I don't want to be the reason for that kind of loss, so silence seems like the only bearable path forward, even with my own year on the line.

There's a tightness in my throat thinking about this. I don't know what they're expecting from me right now, and that gap in understanding is unsettling. What I do know is that if I speak, they serve five years alone, and that's a heavy cost to hand someone. I care what happens to them, even after we go our separate ways. I think I'll stay quiet, though the uncertainty still gnaws at me.

I've gone back and forth so many times my head hurts. Part of me wonders if talking is the safer bet, but then I picture them locked up five extra years because of what I said, and it makes me sick. I can't tell if they'd forgive that or not — there's no way to know their side now. Still, causing that much harm feels wrong to carry, so silence seems like the lesser evil.

This decision keeps me up at night, honestly. They chose to protect me by staying quiet, or maybe they just gave up — I really can't tell which, and it unsettles me not knowing. What's clear is that if I turn on them, they lose five years, a real and heavy loss. I don't think I can live easy knowing I caused that. I'll stay silent too, even though a year still weighs on me.

My nerves are frayed just thinking this through. I don't know what expectations they're holding onto in that other room, and that blind spot makes me uneasy. But I do know that speaking against them means five years taken from their life, a loss I can picture too clearly. Their wellbeing matters to me even if we'll never cross paths again, so I'm leaning toward silence, uncomfortable as this whole thing is.

I feel shaky admitting this, but I think I'd give evidence, and it doesn't sit easy with me. I can't be sure what they're thinking or hoping for right now, which makes the guilt harder to place. I know full well that choosing this means they take on five years alone, a serious loss for them. It's not something I feel good about — it just feels like the only way I get free.

There's a knot in my chest as I think this through. I keep trying to guess what they expect of me, whether silence or betrayal, but I genuinely can't tell, and that not-knowing is unnerving. What I can see plainly is the damage — five years gone if I talk. Their situation matters to me, so I lean toward staying quiet, even knowing my own year won't be easy either.

I'm anxious just writing this down. Their choice to stay silent already sits heavy on me, and I struggle to know if they did it out of loyalty or just resignation — I have no way to be certain. But the harm is obvious to me: five years lost if I speak against them, and that's not a small thing to inflict on someone. I care what happens to them, so silence feels like the only choice I can live with.
